title: Hybrid friendship contact is dominant in Canada, while virtual-only connection is associated with lower satisfaction and greater loneliness
source_unit: Statistics Canada, Survey on Social Connections – Well-being in Canada, 2025
geography: Canada; residents aged 15 and over in the ten provinces, excluding territories, institutions, and First Nations reserves and settlements

observations.period: 2025; friend-contact mode in the previous month and friendship outcomes

denominator.unit: Survey on Social Connections respondents aged 15+; public release does not disclose one pooled respondent count for all displayed estimates

hybrid_virtual_inperson_contact.unit: percent communicating with friends both virtually and in person

virtual_only_contact.unit: percent communicating with friends virtually only

inperson_only_contact.unit: percent communicating with friends in person only

friendship_satisfaction_hybrid.unit: percent satisfied or very satisfied with friendships among people using both modes

friendship_satisfaction_virtual_only.unit: percent satisfied or very satisfied with friendships among people using virtual contact only

friendship_satisfaction_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between hybrid and virtual-only groups

dependable_support_hybrid.unit: percent always or often having people to depend on among hybrid-contact group

dependable_support_virtual_only.unit: percent always or often having people to depend on among virtual-only group

loneliness_hybrid.unit: percent always or often feeling lonely among hybrid-contact group

loneliness_virtual_only.unit: percent always or often feeling lonely among virtual-only group

mechanism.value: Digital communication is usually layered onto in-person contact rather than replacing it; virtual-only connection is associated with lower friendship satisfaction, weaker dependable support, and more loneliness

observations.method: Descriptive extraction from Statistics Canada The Daily release and Table 1; outcome gaps are calculated from published subgroup percentages.
observations.uncertainty: The release explicitly states that associations do not imply causation: people with less satisfying friendships may choose virtual-only contact, and unmeasured distance, health, mobility, work, migration, income, or prior isolation may affect both contact mode and outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Residents aged 15 and over in Canada's ten provinces, by friend-contact mode during the month before the survey.
observations.counterinterpretation: Virtual-only contact may preserve relationships across distance and can be adaptive; lower satisfaction may reflect the circumstances requiring virtual-only contact rather than a harmful effect of technology.

observations.period: 2025; friend-contact mode by income, immigration, racialized group, disability, and age

denominator.unit: Survey on Social Connections respondents aged 15+; subgroup denominators are not disclosed in the public Table 1

virtual_only_recent_immigrants.unit: percent among people who immigrated to Canada in the previous 10 years

recent_immigrant_virtual_only_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between recent immigrants and non-immigrants

virtual_only_low_income.unit: percent among households with income below $40,000

virtual_only_high_income.unit: percent among households with income $150,000 or more

hybrid_low_income.unit: percent among households with income below $40,000

hybrid_high_income.unit: percent among households with income $150,000 or more

mechanism.value: Virtual-only friendship contact is more common among recent immigrants, some racialized groups, and lower-income households, suggesting that digital sociality can be both a bridge across distance and a marker of constrained in-person opportunity

observations.method: Descriptive extraction from Statistics Canada Table 1 and the accompanying The Daily commentary; subgroup differences are calculated from published percentages.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates are self-reported and cross-sectional; racialized-group and immigrant patterns may reflect geography, household structure, distance from family, language, work, discrimination, health, and access to social spaces rather than technology alone.
observations.subgroup: Canadian residents aged 15 and over, by immigration status, racialized group, disability status, age, and household income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Virtual-only communication may be a successful adaptation to migration and distance; income differences may reflect residential geography and opportunity to meet in person rather than digital exclusion.
